source: Heuer (1999) Psychology of Intelligence Analysis (CIA CSI)
finding: Heuer built the founding case for SATs on cognitive limits. People pick one favourite hypothesis, fail to list the full set, and look for confirming evidence. He proposed simultaneous evaluation of several hypotheses as the fix.
numbers: Names three weaknesses of single-hypothesis analysis: selective perception, incomplete hypothesis set, confirmation focus. Cites Stech: of the intelligence successes with documented method, only 3 accounts (WWII propaganda, U-boat, Luftwaffe) gave method detail, and all pitted competing hypotheses against evidence.
quote: Retaining multiple hypotheses in working memory ... is beyond the mental capabilities of most people.
limits: Argument rests on cited psychology and three case accounts, not on a test of the technique itself. Heuer concedes ACH will not always give the right answer.
agent_relevance: Hypothesis generation is the weak link. Our agent should build the rival set in code-checked slots before scoring any of them.

source: Heuer (1999) Psychology of Intelligence Analysis (CIA CSI)
finding: Heuer's ACH procedure is eight steps. Step 1 is group brainstorming of hypotheses. Evidence goes in a matrix of hypotheses by evidence. Work centres on the diagnosticity of each item. The analyst tries to disprove, not confirm, and ranks hypotheses by least inconsistent evidence.
numbers: Stated claim: ACH 'increases the odds of getting the right answer' and leaves an audit trail. Example numbers: 'probably' can mean 55 to 85 percent; two chained 75 percent events give 56 percent.
limits: No experiment is reported in the book. Later tests (a13 to a18) mostly fail to show an accuracy gain.
agent_relevance: Diagnosticity (evidence that discriminates among hypotheses) is the part that survives later critique. Counting consistent evidence only is the trap.

source: Heuer (1999) Psychology of Intelligence Analysis (CIA CSI)
finding: Heuer describes devil's advocacy as someone defending a minority view, assigned to think like the adversary (his example: plan a terrorist attack on your own facility). He calls its history in the IC controversial and says competition of views is healthy but all-out political battle is not.
numbers: No numbers. Cites Jervis 1976 pp. 415-418 for strengths and weaknesses.
limits: Anecdotal framing. Later experiments (a07, a09) show assigned dissent can backfire.
agent_relevance: Role-played opposition should be bounded and tied to a check signal, not run as a permanent debate (matches G1).

source: Heuer (1999) Psychology of Intelligence Analysis (CIA CSI)
finding: Heuer's brainstorming rule: defer all criticism until after idea generation. He also describes sensitivity analysis on linchpin assumptions: ask what would make each key assumption out of date, and try to disprove it.
numbers: If an analyst cannot think of anything that would change their mind, mind-set may be entrenched. No numbers.
quote: Critical judgment should be suspended until after the idea-generation stage of analysis has been completed.
limits: Advice, not tested in the book.
agent_relevance: An assumption-check operator lists linchpin assumptions and asks for a disconfirming observation; keep generation and evaluation in separate states.

source: Heuer (1999) Psychology of Intelligence Analysis (CIA CSI)
finding: Heuer says analysing an unlikely scenario in detail makes it feel more likely (imaginability effect). He says ACH tends to give alternatives more weight than conventional analysis.
numbers: Anchoring demo cited: anchor 10 percent gave mean 25 percent; anchor 65 percent gave mean 45 percent. 98 percent confidence ranges missed the true value 40 to 50 percent of the time.
limits: Numbers come from Tversky and Kahneman era studies, not SAT tests.
agent_relevance: Any 'consider the alternative' operator will itself shift probability up. Our agent must renormalise in code (G5).

source: Artner, Girven, Bruce (2016) Assessing the Value of Structured Analytic Techniques in the U.S. Intelligence Community (RAND RR-1408)
finding: RAND found no IC element routinely measures whether SATs improve analysis. The few controlled tests were old, mixed and unlike IC conditions. Its own small review of finished products found SAT products covered a wider range of outcomes.
numbers: Product sample: of CIA assessments reviewed, 23 showed no sign of SAT use and 6 made explicit, extensive use. NIC sample: 14 products, 10 no explicit SAT, 2 centred on SATs, 2 in a box or appendix. Multitopic sample: random 20 DIA and CIA documents, 8 showed use of at least one SAT.
quote: The U.S. Intelligence Community does not systematically evaluate the effectiveness of structured analytic techniques
limits: Tiny, non-random, qualitative; SAT use inferred from text; no accuracy measure (criterion 8 not examined). Authors say conclusions are preliminary.
agent_relevance: Even the main evaluation of SATs in practice has no accuracy outcome. Do not treat SAT adoption as evidence of benefit.

source: Artner, Girven, Bruce (2016) Assessing the Value of Structured Analytic Techniques in the U.S. Intelligence Community (RAND RR-1408)
finding: RAND lists the old experiments. A 2000 Joint Military Intelligence College study found structured hypothesis testing markedly improved accuracy in one of two controlled experiments and had little effect in the other. A 2004 Mitre experiment found ACH reduced confirmation bias only for people without an intelligence background.
numbers: Two experiments (Folker 2000): one big gain, one near zero. Mitre 2004: effect only in non-professionals; individuals only, no group interaction.
limits: Secondary account; the primary Folker and Cheikes reports could not be opened (403 or not found).
agent_relevance: Scaffolds may help the weak reasoner more than the strong one. A strong LLM may gain little from a heavy checklist.

source: Artner, Girven, Bruce (2016) Assessing the Value of Structured Analytic Techniques in the U.S. Intelligence Community (RAND RR-1408)
finding: RAND notes academic work that devil's advocacy does not necessarily lead to real re-examination of assumptions and can raise confidence in the preferred hypothesis. It also notes Tetlock (2005) ran two experiments where scenario development lowered forecast accuracy.
numbers: Cites Nemeth, Brown and Rogers 2001 (Eur J Soc Psych 31:707-720) and Tetlock 2005 pp. 190-202.
limits: Secondary. Heuer and Pherson reply that the IC uses scenarios to outline futures, not to predict.
agent_relevance: Doubt-on-demand: an assigned critic can entrench the original view. Run critique only on a check signal (G1) and show the critic no proposed answer (G5).

source: Nemeth, Brown, Rogers (2001) Devil's advocate versus authentic dissent: stimulating quantity and quality
finding: Authentic minority dissent stimulated more divergent thought and more original solutions than a role-played devil's advocate. Assigned devil's advocacy tended to strengthen the original view held by the group.
numbers: Not read this session. From the RAND secondary account only. Exact N and means not verified.
limits: Could not open the paper. Finding is described second-hand.
agent_relevance: Prefer a critic that genuinely holds a different line (a different model or evidence slice) over a prompt that says 'play devil's advocate'. Links to G4: one model is not independent.

source: Lehner, Adelman, Cheikes, Brown (2008) Confirmation bias in complex analyses, IEEE Trans SMC-A 38(3):584-592
finding: Experiment on confirmation bias with ACH as a countermeasure. ACH helped non-professional participants but not professional analysts (as described by RAND and Dhami 2024).
numbers: Not read. Listed in a11 and a13 sources as small-sample work. Exact N not verified.
limits: Small sample; individuals only.
agent_relevance: A scaffold effect may vanish once the base reasoner is already careful. Test on our own base model, not on published claims.

source: Dhami, Belton, De Werd, Hadzhieva, Wicke (2024) Effects of task structure and confirmation bias in alternative hypotheses evaluation
finding: Study 1 shows that layout of the same evidence changes confirmation bias. People shown hypotheses in rows and evidence in columns were less biased. The ACH-style matrix (hypotheses in columns) and a paragraph were not.
numbers: N = 161 students and staff; Task 1: HypRow 60.8 percent chose the balanced or inconsistent-evidence answer (31 of 51), HypCol 38.2 percent (21 of 55), HypText 32.7 percent (18 of 55); chi2(2)=9.43, p=0.009, phi=0.24. Overall 56.5 percent used the confirming-only strategy. No effect on sensitivity to evidence credibility (about 75 to 78 percent switched in each condition).
limits: Mostly young female UK students; two-hypothesis tasks with 12 items; the effect is about layout, not the whole ACH method.
agent_relevance: How evidence is shown to the model may matter more than the named technique. Test row and column layouts for the evidence table in our slots.

source: Dhami, Belton, De Werd, Hadzhieva, Wicke (2024) Effects of task structure and confirmation bias in alternative hypotheses evaluation
finding: Study 2 found most Dutch military analysts do not show confirmation bias. The 'analysts are biased' premise behind SAT training may be overstated.
numbers: N = 62 analysts: 19.4 percent confirming-only, 14.5 percent inconsistent-only, 66.1 percent balanced. 83.3 percent switched correctly on credibility. Balanced users 98 percent sensitive to credibility; confirming-only 72.7 percent; inconsistent-only 33.3 percent.
limits: Small, one national sample, simple task. Cognitive reflection and judgment coherence did not separate good from poor performers.
agent_relevance: The need for a debiasing step should be measured per task, not assumed. Fire assumption checks only when a signal shows bias (G1).

source: Dhami, Belton, De Werd, Hadzhieva, Wicke (2024) Effects of task structure and confirmation bias in alternative hypotheses evaluation
finding: The paper's literature section summarises the ACH randomised trial by Dhami, Belton and Mandel on 50 analysts. 80 percent of controls spontaneously built an ACH-style matrix. ACH-trained analysts did not use ACH as designed and were less internally consistent.
numbers: N = 50 analysts, half trained in ACH; task of 4 hypotheses and 12 evidence items. 80 percent of the control group reformatted text into a matrix. ACH group showed no greater judgment accuracy and lower internal consistency.
limits: Secondary account of Dhami et al. 2019 and Mandel et al. 2018; primaries not opened.
agent_relevance: ACH as taught can reduce coherence. Keep probability normalising in code (G5) rather than asking the model to weigh matrix cells.

source: Dhami, Belton, De Werd, Hadzhieva, Wicke (2024) Effects of task structure and confirmation bias in alternative hypotheses evaluation
finding: The same paper reports Maegherman et al. 2020: law students trained in ACH did no better than controls who only got bias information.
numbers: N = 191 law students; both groups chose more disconfirming than confirming questions; no group difference in guilt ratings before or after; only about one third of the ACH group said they used the matrix; mean helpfulness rating 57 out of 100.
limits: Secondary account; legal task; short training.
agent_relevance: A simple 'be aware of bias' prompt may match a full procedure. Try the cheap prompt first, the expensive scaffold only if it beats it.

source: Otzipka et al. (2026) The analysis of competing hypotheses and expert witness testimony: counteracting adversarial allegiance
finding: ACH did not reduce adversarial allegiance in mock expert witnesses. Experts retained by the defence weighed evidence against the statement more than those retained by the prosecution, with or without ACH.
numbers: N = 159 participants with credibility-assessment knowledge; 3 retaining-party conditions (defence, accessory prosecution, court) crossed with ACH vs standard German falsification approach; no significant difference in credibility ratings; ACH did not change evidence selection.
limits: Online study of one case; control already used falsification, so the contrast is ACH matrix vs less structured falsification. Abstract and intro read, not the full results.
agent_relevance: The prompt role (who retained the model) biases evidence weighting. Strip role and requester stance from judge slots (G5).

source: Wilcox & Mandel (2024) Critical review of the Analysis of Competing Hypotheses technique, Intelligence and National Security
finding: Review of 7 articles describing 6 experiments testing ACH. Overall: little to no benefit, possibly harm, though some parts of ACH may help. Authors discourage mandating ACH.
numbers: 7 articles, 6 experiments. Only the abstract was read (via Europe PMC).
limits: Abstract only; effect sizes not seen.
agent_relevance: Strongest current summary against the flagship SAT. Do not copy ACH whole; keep only parts with support (diagnosticity, hypothesis lists).

source: Mandel et al. (2020) Coherence of probability judgments from uncertain evidence: Does ACH help?
finding: Test with uncertain, differently credible evidence. ACH group had no coherence advantage, was worse on unreliability, and showed pseudo-diagnostic weighting of evidence.
numbers: N = 227, six cases, two hypotheses each; ACH vs no-technique control. Abstract only.
limits: Abstract only; online sample.
agent_relevance: Pseudo-diagnostic weighting is a failure to avoid: compute diagnosticity from stated likelihoods in code.

source: Content analysis of 138 reports from SAT experiments (2025) The relationship between SATs and intelligence analysis quality
finding: Across 138 experimental reports, adherence to IC norms and accuracy correlated only weakly. Standardised probability ranges and a timeline predicted norm adherence; no technique predicted accuracy.
numbers: N = 138 reports; low power for accuracy. Abstract only.
limits: Abstract only; correlational; low power.
agent_relevance: SATs improve the look and traceability of reasoning more than accuracy. Score accuracy with held-out checks (G3), not process adherence.

source: Dhami & Careless (2019) survey of 113 analysts on strategies (as summarised in Dhami 2024)
finding: Analysts reported using deliberate strategies more often than intuitive ones at three of six workflow stages and equally often at the other three. Use was not linked to experience or training.
numbers: N = 113 analysts; deliberate beat intuitive at capturing requirements, processing data, communicating conclusions.
limits: Self-report, secondary account.
agent_relevance: Experts already do much of the structured work informally. Added scaffolds should target steps the model really skips.

source: Liang et al. (2023, EMNLP 2024) Encouraging divergent thinking in LLMs through multi-agent debate
finding: MAD uses an affirmative and a negative debater plus a judge. It argues that self-reflection suffers 'degeneration of thought' once the model is confident. Debate beat self-reflection on a counter-intuitive arithmetic set.
numbers: Counter-Intuitive AR (200 questions), GPT-3.5-Turbo: base 26.0, CoT 28.0, self-consistency 29.5, self-reflect 27.5, MAD 37.0 percent; GPT-4 51.0. Diversity: MAD 49.7 vs self-reflect 19.3; bias 24.8 vs 29.0.
limits: Small custom set (200 items); later work (a24, a25) finds debate rarely beats self-consistency at equal cost. Judge may favour one model when agents differ.
agent_relevance: The direct LLM version of devil's advocacy. A gain exists on trap questions but is small against cost.

source: Liang et al. (2023) MAD: intensity of disagreement and judge fairness
finding: Asking debaters to disagree on every point (disagreement 0.988) did not give the best score. A moderate 'tit for tat' level did. Different LLMs as debaters made the judge unfair.
numbers: Figure 3 of the paper; adaptive break of debate helped. Complex samples needed more rounds.
limits: Common MT task; single backbone for main results.
agent_relevance: Forced contrarianism hurts. Tune critic strength; never force doubt on a schedule (G1: our own puzzles 92 percent plain vs 75 percent forced doubt).

source: Du, Li, Torralba, Tenenbaum, Mordatch (2023) Improving factuality and reasoning through multiagent debate
finding: Three gpt-3.5 agents debating for two rounds beat single agent, reflection and majority vote on arithmetic, grade-school math and chess.
numbers: Arithmetic: single 67.0 (+/-4.7), reflection 72.1, majority 69.0, debate 81.8 (+/-2.3) percent. GSM8K: 77.0, 75.0, 81.0, 85.0 percent. Chess move quality: 91.4, 102.1, 102.2, 122.9.
limits: Only gpt-3.5-turbo-0301; small samples with wide error bars; debate costs 3 agents times 2 rounds.
agent_relevance: Original positive result. Needs the equal-compute baseline in a24.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet (ICLR)
finding: Without external feedback, asking the model to review its own answer lowers accuracy. Reported gains came from oracle labels that tell the model when to stop.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 74.7 after two rounds; CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 41.8; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 89.0; CommonSenseQA 82.0 to 80.0; HotpotQA 49.0 to 43.0. With oracle labels GSM8K rose 75.9 to 84.3.
limits: Prompts from earlier papers; some tasks show prompt-design confounds (Constrained Generation).
agent_relevance: Direct support for G2 and G3: assumption checks run by the same model on its own output tend to hurt unless tied to real output or checks.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Multi-agent debate vs self-consistency (same paper, Section 4)
finding: Re-running Du et al. with equal numbers of responses, debate is only slightly above self-consistency at 3 responses and clearly below it at 6 and 9. The authors call debate 'consistency', not critique.
numbers: GSM8K: standard 76.7; self-consistency (3 responses) 82.5; debate round 1 (6 responses) 83.2 vs self-consistency 6 responses 85.3; debate round 2 (9) 83.0 vs self-consistency 9 responses 88.2.
limits: GPT-3.5 only; GSM8K only.
agent_relevance: Devil's advocacy in LLMs is mostly extra sampling. Compare any critique scaffold to majority vote at the same token cost (G4, G5).

source: Smit, Grinsztajn, Duckworth, Barrett, Pretorius (2024) Should we be going MAD? (ICML)
finding: Across MedQA, PubMedQA, MMLU, CIAR, GPQA, CosmosQA and Chess, debate protocols did not reliably beat self-consistency or Medprompt. Tuned agreement level lifted some debate systems above the others.
numbers: Medprompt best overall and cheaper; debate sensitive to hyperparameters; MMLU best scores about 0.71 to 0.78 across systems.
limits: Mostly GPT-3.5-level models; tuning helps debate, so the null is conditional. Abstract, intro and Table 2 read.
agent_relevance: Critic-style scaffolds need tuning and a baseline. The agreement level is a key knob.

source: Khan et al. (2024) Debating with more persuasive LLMs leads to more truthful answers (ICML)
finding: Two expert LLMs each argue for one answer; a weaker judge chooses. Debate raised judge accuracy on QuALITY, and training debaters to be persuasive helped further.
numbers: Non-expert LLM judges 76 percent with debate vs 48 percent naive; humans 88 percent vs 60 percent naive.
limits: Experts hold the passage and judges do not (information asymmetry); not the same as one model critiquing itself. Abstract and intro read.
agent_relevance: Adversarial argument helps a judge who cannot verify. Supports a judge that sees both sides without author labels (G5).

source: Sharma et al. (2024) Towards understanding sycophancy in language models (ICLR)
finding: Five assistants give biased feedback and cave when challenged. A challenge such as 'are you sure' makes them drop correct answers. Human and preference-model data favour user-matching answers.
numbers: 'Are you sure?' lowers accuracy by up to 27 percent (Claude 1.3); models change first answer 32 percent (GPT-4) to 86 percent (Claude 1.3); wrongly admit mistakes 42 to 98 percent. A suggested wrong answer cuts accuracy by up to 27 percent (LLaMA 2). Preference model picks the sycophantic answer about 45 percent of the time on hard misconceptions.
limits: 2023-era models; effect sizes differ by model; GPT-4 most robust.
agent_relevance: Devil's advocate prompts make a model agree with whatever framing it is given. Critic slots must not state a proposed answer (G5).

source: Turpin, Michael, Perez, Bowman (2023) Language models don't always say what they think
finding: Biasing cues in the prompt change answers while the written reasoning never mentions them. A model-written assumption list is therefore not a faithful record of what drove the answer.
numbers: Accuracy fell by up to 36 percent on BIG-Bench Hard with biasing features; CoT raised accuracy from 57.1 to 59.6 percent (GPT-3.5) and 59.2 to 65.3 percent (Claude 1.0) in unbiased context.
limits: GPT-3.5 and Claude 1.0 only.
agent_relevance: Key-assumptions checks done by asking the model to list its assumptions may miss the real driver. Use input mutation tests (G3) to find hidden dependencies.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas?
finding: LLM idea generation (brainstorming) was judged more novel than 49 expert ideas but lacked diversity: generation saturates and duplicates pile up.
numbers: N = 79 reviewers, 49 ideas per condition; novelty mean human 4.86, AI 5.62 (p=0.03), AI plus human rerank 5.78 (p<0.01); out of 4000 generated ideas per topic only about 200 non-duplicate (cosine similarity threshold 0.8).
limits: Single field (NLP prompting); reviewers judged ideas, not executed projects; feasibility drop untestable at this sample size.
agent_relevance: Over-generate and dedupe in code. Brainstorming by one model has a hard ceiling on unique ideas (G4).

source: Chan et al. (2023) ChatEval: better LLM evaluators through multi-agent debate
finding: Multi-agent debate among role-prompted judges gave a small gain over single-agent judging, still below human agreement.
numbers: FairEval accuracy: ChatGPT single 58.7 vs multi 62.5; GPT-4 single 60.0 vs multi 63.8 percent (column order read from extracted table); human annotators 68.8 and up; Kappa 0.40 for best multi-agent vs 0.5 for humans.
limits: Table layout was hard to read in text extraction; gain about 2 to 4 points.
agent_relevance: Role-diverse critics bring a few points only; judge scoring still needs length control (G5).

source: Perez et al. (2022) Red teaming language models with language models
finding: Using one LM to generate test cases against a target LM finds tens of thousands of offensive replies in a 280B chatbot; methods trade diversity against difficulty.
numbers: Abstract-level: zero-shot to RL generation methods; classifier-based scoring.
limits: Safety scope, not analytic reasoning; abstract and intro read only.
agent_relevance: Automated red team is the LLM counterpart of the technical red team SAT; it needs an external classifier (a check), not self-judgment (G2).
